source_text: Referunt aliquando dictum a quodam, cum primum quaestio ista temptata est, Et quomodo ceteras sollicitabimus ad huiusmodi opus? Scilicet felices nos facient, si plures erunt, et non dei gratia vel merita cuiusque. Virgines ecclesiam, an ecclesia virgines ornat deo sive commendat? Confessus est igitur gloriam esse in causa. Porro ubi gloria, illic sollicitatio, ubi sollicitatio, illic coactio, ubi coactio, illic necessitas, ubi necessitas, illic infirmitas. Merito itaque, dum caput non tegunt, ut sollicitentur gloriae causa, ventres tegere coguntur infirmitatis ruina. Aemulatio enim illas, non religio producit. Aliquando et ipse dens venter earum, quia facile virgines fraternitas suscipit. Nec tantum autem ruunt, sed et funem longum delictorum sibi attrahunt. Prolatae enim in medium et publicato bono suo elatae et fratribus omni honore et caritatis operatione cumulatae, dum non labent, ubi quid admissum est, tantum dedecoris cogitant quantum honoris habuerunt. Si intectum caput virginitati adscribitur, si qua virgo exciderit de gratia virginitatis, ne prodatur, intecto permanet capite, et tunc iam alieno ambulat habitu. Consciae mulieritatis iam indubitatae audent nudo capite ad deum adire. Sed aemulator deus et dominus, qui dixit, Nihil occultum quod non revelabitur, plerasque etiam in conspectum deducit. Non enim confitebuntur nisi ipsorum infantium suorum vagitibus proditae. Quantum autem plures, non etiam de pluribus sceleribus suspectas habebis? Dicam, licet nolim, difficile mulier semel fit quae timet fieri, quaeque iam facta potest virginem mentiri sub deo. Quanta item circa uterum suum audebit, ne etiam mater detegatur? Scit deus quot iam infantes et perfici et perduci ad partum integros iuverit debellatos aliquamdiu a matribus. Facillime semper concipiunt et felicissime pariunt huiusmodi virgines, et quidem simillimos patribus. Haec admittit flagitia coacta et invita virginitas. Ipsa concupiscentia non latendi non est pudica. Patitur aliquid quod virginis non sit, studium placendi utique et viris. Quantum velis bona mente conetur, necesse est publicatione sui periclitetur, dum percutitur oculis incertis et multis, dum digitis demonstrantium titillatur, dum nimium amatur, dum inter amplexus et oscula assidua concalescit. Sic frons duratur, sic pudor teritur, sic solvitur, sic discitur aliter iam placere desiderare.
thought_title: The ruin that follows from virgins seeking glory
orientation: Tertullian is answering the objection that veiling virgins will discourage others from embracing virginity, and he now traces the moral ruin that comes when virgins go unveiled for the sake of glory.
pass_a_gloss: They report that it was once said by someone, when this question was first attempted, 'And how shall we encourage the rest to this kind of work?' Of course they will make us happy, if they are more numerous, and not the grace of God or the merits of each one. Do virgins adorn the church, or does the church adorn virgins to God or commend them? He confessed therefore that glory is in the matter. Further, where there is glory, there is solicitation; where there is solicitation, there is compulsion; where there is compulsion, there is necessity; where there is necessity, there is weakness. Deservedly therefore, while they do not cover the head, so that they may be solicited for the sake of glory, they are compelled to cover their bellies by the ruin of weakness. For rivalry, not religion, brings them out. Sometimes also their belly itself is their god, because the brotherhood easily receives virgins. Nor do they only fall, but they also draw to themselves a long rope of sins. For when they have been brought out into public and lifted up by the publicizing of their good and heaped up by the brothers with every honor and with the work of love, while they do not fall, when something has been committed, they think of as much disgrace as they had of honor. If an uncovered head is ascribed to virginity, if any virgin has fallen from the grace of virginity, lest she be betrayed, she remains with uncovered head, and then she now walks in another's dress. Conscious now of undoubted womanhood they dare to go to God with bare head. But God is a rival and Lord, who said, 'Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed,' and he brings very many also into public view. For they will not confess unless betrayed by the wailings of their own infants. But how many more will you not also hold suspect of more crimes? I shall say it, though I would not wish to: a woman is made with difficulty once, who fears to be made one, and she who has already been made one can lie that she is a virgin under God. How many things likewise will she dare around her womb, lest she also be detected as a mother? God knows how many infants, fought against for some time by their mothers, he has helped to be both completed and brought to birth whole. Such virgins most easily always conceive and most happily give birth, and indeed to children most like their fathers. These crimes does compelled and unwilling virginity admit. The very desire of not hiding is not modest. She suffers something that is not of a virgin, the zeal of pleasing certainly also men. However much she may attempt with good mind, it is necessary that she be endangered by the publicizing of herself, while she is struck by uncertain and many eyes, while she is titillated by the fingers of those pointing her out, while she is loved too much, while she grows warm amid embraces and constant kisses. Thus the forehead is hardened, thus modesty is worn away, thus it is loosened, thus she learns to desire to please in another way already.

choices.why: The verb means to stir up or incite; 'encourage' keeps the sense of prompting others to action, matching the objection's concern about recruiting virgins.
Tertullian contrasts rivalry with religion; 'rivalry' captures the competitive, glory-seeking motive he condemns.
The literal 'belly' is needed because Tertullian is alluding to Paul's phrase 'whose god is the belly'; the physical term carries the moral point.
The image is of sins strung together like a rope; keeping 'rope' preserves the vivid metaphor of accumulating guilt.
The Latin 'aemulator' echoes the biblical 'jealous God'; 'rival' keeps the root connection with 'aemulatio' earlier in the passage and the sense of God contending for exclusive devotion.
The noun 'publicatio' means making public; 'publicizing' keeps the active sense of self-exposure that Tertullian condemns.

bible_refs.note: venter earum deus — 'their belly is their god' echoes Paul's 'whose god is the belly'
Nihil occultum quod non revelabitur — 'Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed'

pass_b_english: They report that someone once said, when this question was first raised, "And how shall we solicit the rest to this kind of work?" Of course they will make us happy if there are more of them, and not by God's grace or each one's merits. Do virgins adorn the church to God, or does the church adorn virgins, or commend them? He confessed, then, that glory is at stake. Moreover, where there is glory, there is solicitation; where solicitation, compulsion; where compulsion, necessity; where necessity, weakness. Rightly, therefore, while they do not cover their heads in order to be solicited for the sake of glory, they are compelled to cover their bellies by the ruin of weakness. For rivalry, not religion, brings them out.

Sometimes even their own belly is swollen tight, because the brotherhood readily receives virgins. Nor do they merely fall, but they also drag after themselves a long rope of sins. For when they are brought out into public and lifted up by the publicizing of their good, and heaped up by the brothers with every honor and work of love, while they do not fall, when something has been committed, they think of as much disgrace as they had honor.

If an uncovered head is ascribed to virginity, if any virgin falls from the grace of virginity, lest she be exposed, she remains with uncovered head, and then she walks in a habit that is not her own. Conscious now of undoubted womanhood, they dare to approach God with bare head. But God is a jealous God and Lord, who said, "Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed" (Matthew 10:26), and He brings very many even into public view. For they will not confess unless betrayed by the wailings of their own infants. But the more numerous they are, will you not also suspect them of more crimes? I will say it, though I do not wish to: a woman who fears becoming one hardly becomes one only once, and she who has already become one can lie that she is a virgin under God.

How much will she dare concerning her own womb, lest she also be exposed as a mother? God knows how many infants He has helped to be both completed and brought to birth whole, after being fought against for some time by their mothers. Such virgins always conceive most easily and give birth most happily, and indeed to children most like their fathers. Coerced and unwilling virginity admits these disgraceful acts. The very desire not to hide is not modest. She suffers something that is not a virgin's—the eagerness to please, certainly, even men. However much she may strive with good intention, she must be endangered by the publicizing of herself, while she is struck by uncertain and many eyes, while she is titillated by the fingers of those pointing her out, while she is loved too much, while she grows warm amid embraces and constant kisses. Thus the brow is hardened, thus modesty is worn away, thus she is loosened, thus she learns to desire to please in another way.

problems.quote: Sometimes their belly itself is their god, because the brotherhood readily welcomes virgins.
problems.source_quote: Aliquando et ipse dens venter earum, quia facile virgines fraternitas suscipit.
problems.why: The phrase “is their god” is not present in the Latin; it adds a meaning not in the source.
problems.fix: Sometimes even their own belly is dense, because the brotherhood readily receives virgins.

problems.quote: These disgraceful acts are admitted by coerced and unwilling virginity
problems.source_quote: Haec admittit flagitia coacta et invita virginitas
problems.why: Source says coerced and unwilling virginity COMMITS these disgraceful acts (admittit = lets in/commits), not that the acts are admitted by virginity.
problems.fix: Coerced and unwilling virginity admits these disgraceful acts
problems.ruling: Latin: Haec admittit flagitia ... virginitas = crimes admit forced virginity; English reverses agency.

problems.quote: Do virgins adorn the church to God, or does the church adorn virgins?
problems.source_quote: Virgines ecclesiam, an ecclesia virgines ornat deo sive commendat?
problems.why: The clause “sive commendat” (or commend) is omitted, changing the options presented.
problems.fix: Do virgins adorn the church to God, or does the church adorn virgins, or commend them?
problems.ruling: "sive commendat" ("or commends") is omitted, losing a distinct option from the source question.

edits.old: Sometimes their belly itself is their god, because the brotherhood readily welcomes virgins.
edits.new: Sometimes even their own belly is dense, because the brotherhood readily receives virgins.

edits.old: These disgraceful acts are admitted by coerced and unwilling virginity.
edits.new: Coerced and unwilling virginity admits these disgraceful acts.

edits.old: Do virgins adorn the church to God, or does the church adorn virgins?
edits.new: Do virgins adorn the church to God, or does the church adorn virgins, or commend them?

fixed: Added 'is their god' is not in the Latin; corrected to 'Sometimes even their own belly is dense, because the brotherhood readily receives virgins.'
Changed passive to active to match 'admittit' (commits/admits): 'Coerced and unwilling virginity admits these disgraceful acts.'
Restored omitted 'sive commendat' as 'or commend them'.

problems.why: Dens here means 'close-packed/tight', i.e. belly swelled with pregnancy, not 'dense' in modern sense.
problems.ruling: Latin "dens venter" implies swollen/bulging belly (pregnancy); "dense" misleads, not conveying that sense.

edits.old: Sometimes even their own belly is dense
edits.new: Sometimes even their own belly is swollen tight

fixed: Changed 'dense' to 'swollen tight' for 'dens venter earum', where 'dens' means close-packed/tight, referring to a belly swollen with pregnancy.

problems.quote: a woman is proved with difficulty once she fears to be proved one, and she who has already been proved one can lie that she is a virgin under God
problems.source_quote: difficile mulier semel fit quae timet fieri, quaeque iam facta potest virginem mentiri sub deo
problems.why: 'fit/facta' means 'becomes/has become' a woman, meaning she loses virginity. 'Proved' invents an idea of proof or exposure.
problems.fix: a woman who fears becoming one is hardly made a woman once for all, and she who has already become one can pretend to be a virgin before God

problems.quote: where there is glory, there is encouragement; where encouragement, compulsion
problems.source_quote: ubi gloria, illic sollicitatio, ubi sollicitatio, illic coactio
problems.why: 'Sollicitatio' means enticement or soliciting, with a sense of temptation. 'Encouragement' is positive and breaks the chain toward compulsion and weakness. The same problem affects 'sollicitabimus' and 'sollicitentur'.
problems.fix: where there is glory, there is solicitation; where solicitation, compulsion
problems.ruling: sollicitatio/sollicitabimus/sollicitentur are enticement or importuning; 'encouragement' reverses the slide gloria→sollicitatio→coactio→infirmitas.

problems.quote: while they do not fall, when something has been admitted, they think of as much disgrace as they had honor
problems.source_quote: dum non labent, ubi quid admissum est, tantum dedecoris cogitant quantum honoris habuerunt
problems.why: The clause is garbled. It reads as though they are not falling, which contradicts the point that these girls do fall and then fear disgrace.
problems.fix: so that they may not slip; and when something has been committed, they reckon on as much disgrace as they once had honor
problems.ruling: dum non labent contrasts with ubi quid admissum est (while unfallen vs once they slip); English joins both and contradicts the fall.

edits.old: And how shall we encourage the rest to this kind of work?
edits.new: And how shall we solicit the rest to this kind of work?

edits.old: where there is glory, there is encouragement; where encouragement, compulsion
edits.new: where there is glory, there is solicitation; where solicitation, compulsion

edits.old: in order to be encouraged for the sake of glory
edits.new: in order to be solicited for the sake of glory

edits.old: a woman is proved with difficulty once she fears to be proved one, and she who has already been proved one can lie that she is a virgin under God
edits.new: a woman who fears becoming one hardly becomes one once, and she who has already become one can lie that she is a virgin under God

edits.old: when something has been admitted, they think
edits.new: when something has been committed, they think

fixed: solicitation: changed encouragement/solicited forms to solicitation/solicit/solicited for sollicitabimus/sollicitatio/sollicitentur
fit/facta: changed proved/proved one to becoming/become one for fit/fieri/facta, keeping sub deo as under God
dum non labent/admissum: kept while they do not fall for dum non labent as correct contrast, changed admitted to committed for ubi quid admissum est

problems.quote: But God is a rival and Lord
problems.why: aemulator deus means a jealous or zealous God. "Rival" wrongly makes God a competitor and loses the jealousy that drives the argument.
problems.fix: But God is a jealous God and Lord, who said, "Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed,"

problems.quote: a woman who fears becoming one hardly becomes one once
problems.source_quote: difficile mulier semel fit quae timet fieri
problems.why: Difficile...semel means she hardly falls only once; English says fear keeps her from becoming a woman.
problems.fix: a woman who fears becoming one becomes one only once with difficulty
problems.ruling: "difficile ... semel fit" means she is hardly made one only once, so she repeats. English "hardly becomes one once" reads as rarely even once, which reverses the sense.

problems.quote: But how many more will you not also suspect of more numerous crimes?
problems.source_quote: Quantum autem plures, non etiam de pluribus sceleribus suspectas habebis?
problems.why: Quantum plures means the more numerous they are, not how many more you will fail to suspect.
problems.fix: But the more numerous they are, will you not also suspect them of more crimes?
problems.ruling: "Quantum ... plures" is proportional: the more of them, the more crimes suspected. English "how many more will you not suspect" garbles this and loses "suspectas habebis".

edits.old: But God is a rival and Lord, who said, "Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed"
edits.new: But God is a jealous God and Lord, who said, "Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed"

edits.old: But how many more will you not also suspect of more numerous crimes?
edits.new: But the more numerous they are, will you not also suspect them of more crimes?

edits.old: a woman who fears becoming one hardly becomes one once
edits.new: a woman who fears becoming one hardly becomes one only once

fixed: aemulator deus et dominus: 'rival' misstated jealous God who exposes hidden sin; changed to 'jealous God and Lord'.
Quantum autem plures: correlative 'the more numerous they are' not 'how many more'; changed to conditional suspicion of more crimes.
difficile mulier semel fit quae timet fieri: difficile semel scopes to 'only once' i.e. seldom stops at once; inserted 'only' to fix.

polish.changed: Clarified the speaker and ambiguous phrases, smoothed sentence order, and made pronoun references explicit while preserving every claim and Scripture citation.

notes.quote: They report that someone once said, when this question was first raised, "And how shall we encourage the rest to this kind of work?"
notes.why: Unclear who 'someone' is; likely an opponent or church leader defending unveiled virgins.
notes.fix: Identify the speaker as a defender of the unveiled practice.

notes.quote: Sometimes even their own belly is swollen tight, because the brotherhood readily receives virgins.
notes.why: 'Because' implies causation that doesn't follow; the pregnancy results from sexual sin, not from the brotherhood receiving virgins.
notes.fix: Render as 'even though the brotherhood readily receives virgins' or restructure.

notes.quote: a woman is made with difficulty once she fears to be made one
notes.why: 'A woman is made' is unclear; likely means 'a woman is proved/recognized with difficulty once she fears to be recognized.'
notes.fix: Clarify: 'a woman is recognized with difficulty once she fears to be recognized as one.'

last_rejected.quote: a woman is made with difficulty once she fears to be made one
last_rejected.source_quote: difficile mulier semel fit quae timet fieri
last_rejected.why: Means 'a woman who fears to become one is made with difficulty once'—she who fears becoming a woman is rarely made one only once.
last_rejected.fix: a woman who fears to become one is made one with difficulty only once
last_rejected.ruling: English captures Latin meaning: 'difficile mulier semel fit quae timet fieri' = 'it is difficult for a woman who fears to become one to be made even once'.

last_rejected.quote: Do virgins adorn the church to God, or does the church adorn virgins, or commend them?
last_rejected.source_quote: Virgines ecclesiam, an ecclesia virgines ornat deo sive commendat?
last_rejected.why: Both sides either adorn or commend the other to God; English makes commend a third option and drops “to God” from the church.
last_rejected.fix: Do virgins adorn or commend the church to God, or does the church adorn or commend virgins?
last_rejected.ruling: "deo sive commendat" can fairly be read as 'adorn or commend to God'. The English is clumsy, but the question still asks who adorns or commends whom. No meaning is lost.

last_rejected.quote: a woman who fears becoming one hardly becomes one only once
last_rejected.source_quote: difficile mulier semel fit quae timet fieri
last_rejected.why: “Difficile…semel fit” means she hardly becomes a woman once for all, not that she becomes one more than once.
last_rejected.fix: a woman who fears to become one hardly becomes one once for all
last_rejected.ruling: "difficile ... semel fit" naturally means she hardly becomes a woman only once, i.e. repeatedly. The English "hardly becomes one only once" keeps that sense, and the claim's own gloss agrees with it.
